questions.question: In an extensive-form game, which conditions define a set $h_i$ of decision nodes as an information set of player $i$?
options: Player $i$ moves at every node of $h_i$, and every node of $h_i$ leads to terminal nodes with the same payoffs for her.
The nodes of $h_i$ follow one another on a single path from the root, and player $i$ moves at the first of them.
Player $i$ moves at every node of $h_i$, cannot tell which node of $h_i$ is reached, and has the same actions at each.
Player $i$ moves at every node of $h_i$, cannot tell which node of $h_i$ is reached, and $h_i$ has two or more nodes.

questions.question: Player 2 moves at several decision nodes of an extensive-form game. Can one of these nodes belong to two different information sets of player 2?
options: No: her information sets partition her decision nodes, so each node lies in exactly one.
Yes: a node can lie in one set for each earlier move of others that she might be uncertain about.
Yes: a node lies in a singleton set and also in any larger set that contains it.
No: each information set of a player may contain at most one of her decision nodes.

questions.question: An incumbent observes that entry occurred but not whether the entrant is "ready" or "unready"; both of her nodes lie in one information set, with actions Fight and Accommodate. Which statement about her possible plans is correct?
options: She may fight at the unready node and accommodate at the ready one, since each node is a decision node.
She chooses one action for both nodes, so "fight only if unready" is not a plan she can carry out.
She may choose different actions at the two nodes, provided she randomizes at each of them.
She has four pure strategies, choosing one of the two actions separately at each of the two nodes.

questions.question: In an extensive-form game, a player's decision node $x$ forms an information set $\{x\}$ on its own. What does this tell us about the player when she moves at $x$?
options: She knows exactly which node she is at, so she knows all earlier moves leading to $x$.
She knows only her own earlier moves, and none of the earlier moves of her opponents or of Nature.
She moves only once in the whole game, so $x$ is her only decision node.
She has only one action available at $x$, so her choice there is forced.

questions.question: When an extensive-form game is drawn, several decision nodes of one player are placed in the same information set. What do these nodes typically differ in?
options: Only in the payoffs she receives later, which she cannot see before the game ends.
Only in the actions available to her, which she learns when play reaches the node.
Only in events the player did not see, such as a rival's earlier move or a move of Nature.
Only in the time at which she moves, since nodes reached at the same date are grouped together.

questions.question: In an extensive-form game, player $i$ has three information sets, with $3$, $2$ and $4$ actions respectively. In the play that actually occurs, two of these sets are never reached. How many pure strategies does player $i$ have?

Player 2 has two singleton information sets, each with the same $3$ actions. The modeller then removes an observation, merging the two nodes into one information set. How do player 2's pure strategies change in number?
options: From $6$ to $3$.
From $9$ to $3$.
From $9$ to $6$.
From $3$ to $9$.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $H$ or $T$; player 2 then chooses $H$ or $T$. Player 2 wins (payoff $1$, player 1 gets $-1$) when the coins differ, and loses ($-1$, player 1 gets $1$) when they match. Player 2 observes player 1's coin, and her strategies are written (action after $H$, action after $T$). What happens if player 2 uses $(H,T)$?
options: She plays $H$ first and $T$ later, so she wins exactly one of the two rounds.
She wins whatever player 1 does, since her reply always differs from his coin.
She plays $H$ if player 1 plays $T$, so she wins only when player 1 chooses $T$.
She matches player 1's coin every time, so she loses whatever player 1 does.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $L$ or $R$. After $L$, player 2 can choose $l$ or $r$; after $R$, she can choose $l$, $m$ or $r$. A modeller puts player 2's two nodes into one information set. Is this a valid information set?
options: No: the action sets differ, so seeing whether $m$ is available would reveal her node.
Yes: player 2 moves at both nodes, which is all an information set requires.
Yes: it is valid as long as player 2 does not observe whether player 1 chose $L$ or $R$.
No: an information set may only contain nodes that offer exactly two actions.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $L$ or $R$, then player 2 moves, then player 1 moves again. A modeller puts player 1's second-move node after $L$ and her second-move node after $R$ into one information set. Why does this violate perfect recall?
options: Perfect recall forbids any information set that contains more than one node.
Player 1 moves twice, and under perfect recall each player may move only once.
The nodes differ in player 1's own earlier action, which she would have to forget.
The nodes follow different actions of player 2, and under perfect recall player 1 must see them.

questions.question: In an extensive-form game, could one information set contain a decision node of player 1 and a decision node of player 2?
options: Yes: if neither player observes the other, their nodes are grouped together.
Yes: in a simultaneous move both players share a single information set.
No: but only because the two players' payoffs differ at those nodes.
No: one player $i$ moves at every node of an information set $h_i$.

questions.question: A simultaneous-move game in which player 1 has $3$ actions and player 2 has $2$ actions is written as an extensive-form game with player 1 moving first. How many nodes are in player 2's information set, and how many pure strategies does she have?
options: $3$ nodes and $8$ pure strategies.
$2$ nodes and $2$ pure strategies.
$3$ nodes and $2$ pure strategies.
$1$ node and $6$ pure strategies.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $A$, $B$, $C$ or $D$. Player 2 learns only whether the choice was in $\{A,B\}$ or in $\{C,D\}$, and at each of her information sets chooses $x$, $y$ or $z$. How many pure strategies does player 2 have?

Player 1 chooses one of $2$ actions; player 2 observes it and chooses one of $2$ actions; player 3 then chooses without observing either earlier move. How many decision nodes does player 3's information set contain?

In an extensive-form game with perfect recall, player 1 moves at node $x$, and one of her actions there leads, after a move of player 2, to another node $y$ of player 1. Can $x$ and $y$ lie in the same information set?
options: Yes: if she does not observe player 2's move, she cannot tell whether she is at $x$ or $y$.
Yes: provided the same actions are available at $x$ and $y$, the grouping is consistent.
No: the only reason is that $x$ and $y$ are separated by a move of a different player.
No: at $y$ she has already acted at $x$, and remembering that lets her tell $y$ from $x$.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $H$ or $T$; player 2 then chooses $H$ or $T$. Player 2 wins (payoff $1$, player 1 gets $-1$) when the coins differ, and loses ($-1$, player 1 gets $1$) when they match. Compare two versions: in one player 2 does not observe player 1's coin, in the other she does. In each version, how many of player 2's pure strategies win against every choice of player 1?
options: $1$ without observing, $1$ with observing.
$0$ without observing, $2$ with observing.
$0$ without observing, $4$ with observing.
$0$ without observing, $1$ with observing.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses one of $2$ actions. Player 2 observes it and chooses one of $3$ actions. Player 3 then observes player 1's action but not player 2's, and chooses one of $2$ actions. How many pure-strategy profiles $(s_1,s_2,s_3)$ does the game have?

A tree shows player 1 choosing $H$ or $T$, followed by a node of player 2 after each choice; player 2's two nodes are joined by a dashed line, and at each she chooses $H$ or $T$. What does the dashed line mean?
options: Player 2 observes player 1's choice but must pick the same action after $H$ as after $T$.
Player 1 cannot observe player 2's later choice, so the line describes player 1's information, not player 2's.
Player 2 chooses randomly between $H$ and $T$ with equal probabilities at both of her nodes.
Player 2 chooses without observing player 1's choice, so the tree represents simultaneous choices.

questions.question: Nature first draws one of two weather states. Player 1 observes the weather and then chooses from the same set of actions whatever the weather is. Player 2 learns only player 1's action, not the weather, and then moves. Does this extensive-form game have perfect information?
options: No: player 2's nodes that differ only in the weather lie in one non-singleton information set.
Yes: player 2 observes every move made by a player, and unobserved moves of Nature do not count.
Yes: player 1 observes the weather, and it is enough that one player knows each move.
No: any game containing a move by Nature has imperfect information automatically.

questions.question: In Matching Pennies drawn as a tree, player 2 first moves without observing player 1 (one information set, strategies $H$ and $T$). Then her two nodes become singletons, giving the plans $(H,H),(H,T),(T,H),(T,T)$, written (after $H$, after $T$). How do her old strategies relate to the new plans?
options: Each old strategy survives as a constant plan, $(H,H)$ or $(T,T)$; the others are new.
None of the old strategies survives, since every new plan conditions on player 1's coin.
The old strategy $H$ becomes $(H,T)$ and $T$ becomes $(T,H)$, the plans reacting to the coin.
The old strategies become $(H,T)$ and $(T,H)$, since a plan must use both actions.
